coach_says: Taking on a5 with the b-pawn wins the pawn back, but it opens the b-file, and White's rook goes straight to b1 and b7 to hit c7 and your 7th rank. First play c6: it kicks the rook off d5 with tempo, and then you can take a5 with the rook, keeping the b-file closed. Before recapturing, ask which files the capture opens and whose rook gets there first.
concept: opened a file for their rook
also: kick the rook with tempo first

coach_says: Qf3 piles up on f7, but Black has already castled, so f7 is guarded by the rook and king and the attack goes nowhere. Worse, your queen now sits on the knight's retreat square: after ...h6 the g5 knight is short of squares, and ...Nd4 hits the queen and c2 at the same time. Once your opponent has castled, stop aiming at f7 and finish developing with moves like c3, Nc3 or castling.
also: knight on g5 runs out of squares

coach_says: Both captures win the pawn back, but after Bxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 your knight ends up on d5 with nothing guarding it and your king still in the centre. White plays Bg5, hitting your queen with tempo, then Be4 hits the loose knight, and the e-file opens against your king. Recapture with the knight (Nxd5) instead: if White trades on d5 your bishop recaptures, and you can castle quickly.

The a-file is the only open file, and both rooks are staring at each other on it. Take first with Rxa8: after Qxa8 you can develop with Ne2 and castle, and you are a pawn up. f4 does nothing for your development and lets Black take on a1, drag your bishop into the corner and grab the file with ...Qa8, while also opening the long diagonal that f3 used to block. When an open file appears, decide who controls it before making quiet pawn moves.

Your bishop was attacked, but retreating is not the only answer. dxe5 opens the d-file so your queen on d2 attacks the knight on d5, which has no defender: if Black takes your bishop with ...gxh4, Qxd5 wins the knight back with a much better position. After Bg3 Black gets ...e4 and gains space with tempo. When a piece is attacked, first look for a counterattack on something loose.

Your bishop on c1 was the only guard of b2. After Bf4, ...Qxb2 attacks your rook on a1 and the knight on c3, which is already hit by the bishop on d4. Be3 develops just as well and challenges that strong d4 bishop, so a grab on b2 would just lose a piece to Bxd4. Before moving a piece, check what it was protecting.

Against 1...d5 the simple and best answer is to take the pawn with exd5. f3 does not develop anything, takes the best square from your king's knight and loosens the squares around your king. In the opening, prefer captures and developing moves over pawn moves that only defend.
concept: weakening pawn move instead of developing

coach_says: There is a lot of tension in the centre, and Bb4 does not resolve it. White can play exd5 and after ...cxd5 hit back with d4, opening the centre while your d5 pawn becomes a target for the g2 bishop and the c4 pawn. Take on e4 yourself (dxe4) or push ...d4 to gain space; decide what happens to the centre before White does.

Your d5 pawn had no defender: your bishop on d7 blocks the queen from guarding it, and the knight on c3 attacks it. After fxe5, White simply plays Nxd5 and wins it. Each move, check which of your pawns are attacked and how many times they are defended; here ...g4, hitting the f3 knight first, was the active way to handle it.

In the Advance Caro-Kann your light-squared bishop wants to come out to f5 before you play ...e6. Playing ...f5 puts a pawn on that very square, so the bishop on c8 gets shut in, and it also leaves e6 and your king weaker. Play ...Bf5 first, then ...e6 and ...c5 to hit White's centre.
c4 is a perfectly good move, heading into an English or King's Indian type position. Keep developing with d4, Nc3 and e4 or g3.
Nge7 is fine: it guards the c6 knight so that Bxc6 no longer wins the e5 pawn, and it keeps your pieces together. Bd6 was an equally good way to protect e5.
Bb4 is a reasonable developing move. Be aware of Qb3 hitting b7 and the bishop on b4, which ...Nc6 handles, but this is close to the best moves.
Bc4 is playable. Black can blunt the bishop with ...e6 and ...d5, so Nf3 and d4 is the more flexible plan, but the difference is small.
Be7 is fine, though it spends a tempo retreating. Taking on d2 or dropping back to d6 were slightly better, but the position stays balanced.
a5 is one of the best moves: your queenside pawns, supported by the king and bishop, are what win this ending. Keep pushing them while the knight is far away on e2.
Qg3+ is the best move: it checks and picks up the f3 pawn next, opening White's king further while your h-pawn advances. Well played.
Kb7 wins the a7 pawn and keeps the a-pawn rolling, which is winning. Nd6+ was slightly cleaner, but your move does the job.
Qe7 is a reasonable move in a position that is already a bit worse for you after the opening. The top moves (Rg8, c6, Qg5) are only marginally better.
Bb5+ is the best move: after ...c6 that pawn is pinned to the king by your bishop, so it cannot defend d5 and Qxd5 wins the knight. Good use of a check to create a pin.
